🌾 Comparing the Tithing Agent to the Teruma Agent

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing Perek Ma'aser Behema — and the Tractate
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 61a
overview.hebrewSource: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ מַעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה, וּסְלִיקָא לַהּ מַסֶּכֶת בְּכוֹרוֹת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The final daf resolves the three-way tannaitic dispute from the previous daf over what happens to two animals that emerged together as the tenth and were both called 'tenth': one view has them graze until blemished, one has them sacrificed, and one has them put to death. The Gemara assigns each ruling to a different tanna's broader position, then explains that the 'they must die' ruling actually addresses animal tithe in the present era, when consecrated animals cannot be sacrificed and pose a risk of misuse. The daf's final topic turns practical: if one sends an agent to tithe his flock and the agent makes a naming error, whose mistake is it — comparing this case to an agent sent to separate teruma. With this, Bekhorot's final perek, and the entire tractate, concludes.

slides.title: 🌱 Three Fates for the Intermingled Pair
slides.subtitle: Reconciling three baraitot that seem to contradict each other

boxes.title: They Graze
items: One may not bring sacrifices into a situation of likely disqualification
Both would need eating within the STRICTER of tithe's and peace-offering's time limits — risking disqualification

boxes.title: They Are Sacrificed
items: He permits bringing sacrifices even into a situation of likely disqualification

boxes.title: They Must Die
items: Follows Rabbi Yehuda: a mistaken tithe designation has the status of a SUBSTITUTE animal
And a substitute for animal tithe itself must be left to die

slides.title: 💀 But Does Rabbi Yehuda Really Hold Substitutes Die?
slides.subtitle: A challenge from the earlier mishna and its resolution

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: The mishna quotes Rabbi Meir describing R' Yehuda's own view: 'if it were a substitute, it would NOT be sacrificed' — implying R' Yehuda actually holds it IS sacrificed, not put to death!

lines.speaker: Further proof
lines.text: A Sifra baraita (unattributed = Rabbi Yehuda) explicitly derives that the eleventh animal, mistakenly called tenth, is included in 'if his offering be a peace offering' — meaning it's sacrificed.

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, before Rabbi Yoḥanan: the 'they must die' baraita is NOT about ordinary times — it's specifically about animal tithe TODAY, when there's no Temple to sacrifice in.

lines.speaker: Why not just one?
lines.text: The baraita specifies TWO animals (not one) because with only one animal there's no great loss in simply waiting for a blemish — but with two, the greater loss might tempt people to keep them, so the ruling stresses: even so, they must die.

slides.title: 💀 Why Nowadays Specifically Requires Death
slides.subtitle: Connecting back to the broader theme of consecration without a Temple

nodes.content: 🏛️ Without a Temple, animals with sacrificial-level sanctity cannot be brought as offerings
⚠️ Leaving them to graze until blemished risks misuse — shearing, labor, or premature eating, echoing the 'mishap' concern from daf 53
☠️ For animals with the elevated, sacrifice-eligible sanctity of the mistakenly-designated eleventh, the Sages require they be left to die immediately

slides.subtitle: Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa on tithing by proxy
rows: NOT sanctified (owner would never accept losing an entire extra animal)

slides.title: 🌾 Comparing to the Teruma Agent — and Closing the Tractate
slides.subtitle: Why tithing errors differ from teruma-separation errors

steps.content: 1️⃣ Challenge: an agent sent to separate teruma acts on his own judgment of the owner's generosity — even guessing wrong, his teruma is valid
2️⃣ Answer: with teruma, there's a RANGE of acceptable amounts (generous to stingy) — the owner implicitly authorized any reasonable guess
3️⃣ With animal tithe, a naming error isn't a matter of differing legitimate judgment — it's simply a MISTAKE, which the owner never authorized
4️⃣ With this final exchange, the Gemara concludes Perek Ma'aser Behema — and the entire Tractate Bekhorot

callout.label: הדרן עלך:
callout.text: The daf ends with the traditional formula marking both the close of this perek and the completion of the whole tractate.

summary.principle: Even a mistaken designation of animal tithe carries real halakhic consequences — sacrificed, left to graze, or (in the Temple's absence) required to die — and an agent's tithing error, unlike a teruma agent's reasonable estimate, was never authorized by the one who sent him.

flowSteps.content: 🌱 Three baraitot on intermingled animals (graze/sacrifice/die) are each mapped to a different tanna
💀 The 'must die' ruling is reinterpreted as addressing animal tithe specifically in the post-Temple era

columns.content: 📨 An agent's tithing mistake does not bind the owner — unlike a teruma agent's legitimate estimate
🏁 The final exchange closes Perek Ma'aser Behema and Tractate Bekhorot

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: consecration errors are treated seriously throughout Bekhorot — precision, genuine intent, and real transfer of value govern every stage, from a firstborn's birth to the tithe's final count

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution, which tanna's view underlies the baraita ruling that two intermingled animals (the tenth and the mistakenly-designated eleventh) must be put to death?
o: The first tanna of the mishna
Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Yehuda, who holds a mistaken tithe designation has the status of a substitute animal that must die
Rabbi Akiva
quiz.e: The Gemara attributes the 'must die' ruling to Rabbi Yehuda's position that a mistakenly designated animal has the halakhic status of a substitute (temurah), and Rabbi Yehuda holds that a substitute for animal tithe is left to die.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Shimon bar Abba resolve the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda's view that the eleventh animal is sacrificed (proven from a Sifra baraita) and another baraita saying such animals must die?
o: He says the two baraitot simply contradict each other with no resolution
He explains the 'must die' baraita is specifically discussing animal tithe in the present era, without a Temple, when the animals cannot be sacrificed at all
He says Rabbi Yehuda changed his opinion later in life
He claims one baraita is a forgery
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba clarifies that the ruling requiring death applies specifically to animal tithe nowadays, when there's no Temple to bring the animal as an offering, distinguishing it from Rabbi Yehuda's general position that such an animal would otherwise be sacrificed.

quiz.q: Why does the baraita about animals dying nowadays specifically discuss a case of TWO animals, rather than just one?
o: Because the ruling only applies when there are exactly two animals

It uses the style of 'it is not necessary to say': with one animal there's little loss in waiting, but with two the greater potential loss might tempt people to keep them anyway — so the ruling stresses that even then, they must die
Because two animals can never be confused with each other
There is no significance to the number two
quiz.e: The Gemara explains the baraita teaches a stronger case: even where the financial loss from destroying two animals (rather than one) is significant, the concern for mishap still requires that they be put to death.

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa, if a person's agent makes an error in tithing on his behalf — for instance calling the ninth animal 'tenth' — is that animal sanctified?
o: Yes, always, since the agent has full authority
No — Rav Pappa holds it is not sanctified at all, since the owner can say 'I sent you to benefit me, not to harm me'
Only if the agent is a relative
Only if the owner later approves
quiz.e: Rav Pappa disagrees with Rav Pappi and holds that even a minor naming error by the agent does not create sanctity, because the owner's authorization to act as agent doesn't extend to actions that work to his detriment.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara distinguish an agent's mistake in tithing animals from an agent's estimate when separating teruma?
o: There is no meaningful difference between the two cases
With teruma there is a legitimate range of acceptable amounts the owner implicitly authorized; with animal tithe, a naming error is simply a mistake the owner never authorized
Teruma agents are always more trustworthy
Animal tithe agents require special training that teruma agents don't
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that since teruma can validly be given at various levels of generosity, the owner is understood to have authorized the agent's reasonable estimate; but a tithing naming error isn't a matter of legitimate judgment — it's a plain mistake, which falls outside the scope of the agent's authorization.
